key_terms.meaning: ∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx = limit of Σ f(xᵢ*) Δx as the number of subintervals → ∞; a number, not a function
Σᵢ₌₁ⁿ f(xᵢ*) Δx, the sum of rectangle areas that converges to the definite integral
Part 1: d/dx ∫ₐˣ f(t) dt = f(x); Part 2: ∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx = F(b) − F(a) where F′ = f
∫ₐᵇ F′(x) dx = F(b) − F(a): the integral of a rate gives the total change
F is an antiderivative of f when F′(x) = f(x) on an interval
∫ f(x) dx = F(x) + C, the whole family of antiderivatives, C any constant
∫ u dv = uv − ∫ v du, the integral form of the product rule
∫ f(g(x)) g′(x) dx = ∫ f(u) du with u = g(x), the integral form of the chain rule
Writing a rational function as a sum of simple fractions such as A/(x−a) so each piece integrates to a log or a power

key_terms.term: Improper integral of the first kind
key_terms.meaning: ∫ₐ^∞ f(x) dx = lim_{b→∞} ∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx; the interval is infinite

key_terms.term: Improper integral of the second kind
key_terms.meaning: Defined by a limit when f blows up at an endpoint, e.g. ∫₀¹ x^(−p) dx = lim_{c→0⁺} ∫_c¹ x^(−p) dx
The defining limit exists and is finite; otherwise the integral diverges
∫₁^∞ dx/x^p converges for p > 1 and diverges for p ≤ 1; ∫₀¹ dx/x^p converges for p < 1
Γ(n) = ∫₀^∞ x^(n−1) e^(−x) dx for n > 0, with Γ(n+1) = nΓ(n) and Γ(n+1) = n! for whole n
B(m,n) = ∫₀¹ x^(m−1)(1−x)^(n−1) dx = Γ(m)Γ(n)/Γ(m+n) for m, n > 0
A = ∫ₐᵇ [y_upper(x) − y_lower(x)] dx, with a and b the intersection x-values
L = ∫ₐᵇ √(1 + (dy/dx)²) dx, or L = ∫ √((dx/dt)² + (dy/dt)²) dt for a parametric curve
V = π∫ₐᵇ [R(x)]² dx for a solid with no hole, V = π∫ₐᵇ ([R(x)]² − [r(x)]²) dx when there is a hole of radius r
S = 2π∫ₐᵇ y √(1 + (dy/dx)²) dx when the curve y = f(x) is rotated about the x-axis

takeaways: A definite integral is a limit of sums, so it always measures an accumulated quantity such as area, distance or work.
The fundamental theorem is the bridge: differentiating and integrating are inverse operations, and ∫ₐᵇ f = F(b) − F(a) turns a limit into arithmetic.
An indefinite integral is not a single function; the +C records that every antiderivative differs from every other by a constant.
Every integration technique is a differentiation rule read backwards: substitution undoes the chain rule, parts undoes the product rule, partial fractions undoes a common denominator.
An improper integral is defined by a limit; it is said to converge only when that limit is a finite number.
The gamma and beta functions turn many awkward definite integrals into factorial and ratio arithmetic, and B(m,n) = Γ(m)Γ(n)/Γ(m+n) links the two.
For area, always integrate upper minus lower; for volume, always square the radius; the difficulty is choosing the slice, not doing the integral.
Arc length, volume and surface area all come from the same move: cut the object into thin pieces, write the piece length or area, then integrate.
Choose the variable of integration to match the slice: dx for vertical slices, dy for horizontal slices, and pick whichever gives simpler limits.
bank_note: Long answers here are usually full evaluations: set up the limit or the definite integral, show the substitution or the reduction step, and quote the standard results Γ(n+1) = nΓ(n), Γ(1/2) = √π and B(m,n) = Γ(m)Γ(n)/Γ(m+n) by name before using them.

bank.q: Define an improper integral of the first kind and of the second kind. Give one example of each and state what it means for such an integral to converge.
outline: First kind: infinite interval, written as lim_{b→∞} ∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx (and split at an interior point if both ends are infinite).
Second kind: integrand has an infinite discontinuity at an endpoint or interior point, written as a one-sided limit, e.g. lim_{c→0⁺} ∫_c¹ x^(−1/2) dx.
If the limit is a finite number the integral converges and equals that number; if the limit fails to exist or is infinite it diverges.
Examples: ∫₁^∞ dx/x² = 1 (converges); ∫₀¹ dx/x diverges.

bank.q: State both parts of the fundamental theorem of calculus. Explain how the definite integral is defined as a limit of Riemann sums and how the net change theorem follows.
outline: Part 1: if f is continuous, then F(x) = ∫ₐˣ f(t) dt satisfies F′(x) = f(x); differentiating an accumulation function returns the rate.
Part 2: if F is any antiderivative of f on [a,b], then ∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx = F(b) − F(a).
Riemann sum: divide [a,b] into n parts of width Δx = (b−a)/n, pick xᵢ* in each part, and take the limit of Σ f(xᵢ*) Δx.
Net change: ∫ₐᵇ F′(x) dx = F(b) − F(a) says the integral of a rate of change is the total change; example, integrating velocity gives displacement.

bank.q: Write down the standard formulas for arc length, volume of a solid of revolution (disk and washer), and area of a surface of revolution, defining every symbol used.
outline: Arc length: L = ∫ₐᵇ √(1 + (dy/dx)²) dx; parametric form L = ∫ √((dx/dt)² + (dy/dt)²) dt.
Disk: V = π∫ₐᵇ [R(x)]² dx when rotating y = R(x) about the x-axis.
Washer: V = π∫ₐᵇ ([R(x)]² − [r(x)]²) dx, R outer radius, r inner radius.
Surface: S = 2π∫ₐᵇ y √(1 + (dy/dx)²) dx about the x-axis, and 2π∫ₐᵇ x √(1 + (dy/dx)²) dx about the y-axis.
Say clearly that the square root is the length of a small chord, not the function value, and name the limits.

bank.q: Evaluate (a) ∫ x² e^x dx and (b) ∫ dx / ((x+1)(x+2)). Name the technique used in each case.
outline: (a) Apply integration by parts twice: u = x², dv = e^x dx, then again on ∫ 2x e^x dx; answer e^x(x² − 2x + 2) + C.
(b) Partial fractions: 1/((x+1)(x+2)) = 1/(x+1) − 1/(x+2).
Integrate to log |x+1| − log |x+2| + C, i.e. log |(x+1)/(x+2)| + C.
State that the +C is present because the integral is indefinite, and check by differentiating.

bank.q: Using the gamma function, evaluate ∫₀^∞ x⁴ e^(−x) dx and ∫₀^∞ √x e^(−x) dx.
outline: Quote Γ(n) = ∫₀^∞ x^(n−1) e^(−x) dx for n > 0.
First integral is Γ(5) = 4! = 24; show the match of exponents.
Second integral is Γ(3/2) = (1/2)Γ(1/2) = √π/2, using Γ(n+1) = nΓ(n) and Γ(1/2) = √π.
Do not write 4! until the whole number n has been identified in Γ(n+1) = n!.

bank.q: Using the beta function, evaluate ∫₀^(π/2) sin⁵x cos⁴x dx.
outline: Use ∫₀^(π/2) sin^m x cos^n x dx = (1/2) B((m+1)/2, (n+1)/2) for m, n > −1.
Here m = 5, n = 4, so the value is (1/2) B(3, 5/2).
Final answer 8/315; the √π cancels, so show that cancellation.

bank.q: Find the area of the region enclosed between the curves y² = 4x and x² = 4y.
outline: Find intersection points: solve simultaneously to get (0,0) and (4,4).
On 0 ≤ x ≤ 4 the upper curve is y = 2√x and the lower is y = x²/4.
Set up A = ∫₀⁴ (2√x − x²/4) dx.
Antiderivative (4/3)x^(3/2) − x³/12, evaluated to give 32/3 − 16/3 = 16/3 square units.
State units and note that upper minus lower is essential for a positive answer.

bank.q: Find the arc length of the curve y = (2/3)x^(3/2) from x = 0 to x = 3.
outline: Compute dy/dx = x^(1/2), so (dy/dx)² = x.
Set up L = ∫₀³ √(1 + x) dx.
Integrate: (2/3)(1 + x)^(3/2) from 0 to 3.
Value (2/3)(8 − 1) = 14/3 units; check the integrand is continuous on [0,3].

bank.q: The region bounded by y = x², y = 4 and x ≥ 0 is rotated about the y-axis. Find the volume of the solid using washers or disks.
outline: Choose horizontal slices: the variable is y and y runs from 0 to 4.
At height y the horizontal slice is a disk of radius x = √y, since y = x² inverted gives x = √y.
V = π∫₀⁴ (√y)² dy = π∫₀⁴ y dy.
V = π[y²/2]₀⁴ = 8π cubic units.
Explain why dy was chosen: the axis of rotation is vertical, so slices perpendicular to it are horizontal.

bank.q: Discuss the convergence of ∫₁^∞ dx/x^p and ∫₀¹ dx/x^p for all real values of p.
outline: It converges exactly when 1 − p < 0, that is p > 1, with value 1/(p − 1); p = 1 gives log b → ∞, divergence.
Near zero, ∫_c¹ x^(−p) dx = (1 − c^(1−p))/(1 − p), which converges exactly when p < 1.
Summary: infinity needs a fast enough decay (p > 1), a blow-up at zero needs a mild enough one (p < 1); call these the p-test.
Use the comparison test to extend the result to integrands bounded by a multiple of x^(−p).

bank.q: Prove that Γ(n+1) = nΓ(n) for n > 0, deduce Γ(n+1) = n! for whole n, and show Γ(1/2) = √π.
outline: Start from Γ(n+1) = ∫₀^∞ x^n e^(−x) dx and integrate by parts with u = x^n, dv = e^(−x) dx.
The boundary term x^n e^(−x) vanishes at 0 and at ∞ for n > 0, leaving n∫₀^∞ x^(n−1) e^(−x) dx = nΓ(n).
With Γ(1) = ∫₀^∞ e^(−x) dx = 1, induction gives Γ(n+1) = n!.
For Γ(1/2), substitute x = t² in Γ(1/2) = ∫₀^∞ x^(−1/2) e^(−x) dx to reach 2∫₀^∞ e^(−t²) dt.
Evaluate the Gaussian integral (by squaring and using polar coordinates) to get Γ(1/2) = √π.

bank.q: Prove that B(m,n) = Γ(m)Γ(n)/Γ(m+n) for m > 0, n > 0, and hence evaluate ∫₀¹ x³(1 − x)² dx.
outline: Write Γ(m)Γ(n) as a double integral over the first quadrant and substitute x = u v, y = u(1 − v) with Jacobian u.
The u-integral gives Γ(m+n) and the v-integral gives B(m,n); rearrange.
Alternatively derive it in the form B(m,n) = ∫₀^∞ t^(m−1)/(1+t)^(m+n) dt.
Check the answer by direct expansion of x³(1 − x)².

bank.q: The region bounded by y = x² and y = x is rotated about the x-axis. Find the area of the region and the volume of the solid generated, and explain how the two set-ups differ.
outline: Intersections: x² = x gives x = 0 and x = 1, so the interval is [0,1].
Volume by washers: outer radius R = x, inner radius r = x², so V = π∫₀¹ (x² − x⁴) dx.
State the difference: area integrates a difference of lengths, volume integrates a difference of squared lengths; both use upper minus lower.

bank.q: Evaluate ∫₀^∞ dx/(1 + x²) by substitution and a limit, justify each step with the fundamental theorem and the definition of an improper integral, and state whether the integral converges.
outline: Write the integral as lim_{b→∞} ∫₀^b dx/(1 + x²), by definition of an improper integral of the first kind.
Use the antiderivative arctan x, justified by the fundamental theorem since 1/(1 + x²) is continuous on [0,b].
Get arctan b − arctan 0 = arctan b.
Take the limit using arctan b → π/2 as b → ∞.
The integral converges to π/2; note the integrand is positive and bounded, so no singularity arises.

glossary.def: The function f(x) being integrated in ∫ f(x) dx.
The numbers a and b in ∫ₐᵇ that fix the interval of integration.
A finite sum Σ f(xᵢ*) Δx of rectangle areas that approximates a definite integral.
The limit of Riemann sums over an interval; a single number.
A function F whose derivative equals the given function f.
The family F(x) + C of all antiderivatives of f.
The arbitrary constant C added to an indefinite integral.
The pair of results linking differentiation and integration as inverse processes.
The statement that the integral of a derivative over an interval equals the total change of the function.
Change of variable that reverses the chain rule in integration.
Rule ∫ u dv = uv − ∫ v du that reverses the product rule.
Rewriting a rational function as a sum of simpler fractions before integrating.
An integral defined as a limit because the interval is infinite or the integrand is unbounded.
The property that the defining limit of an improper integral exists and is finite.
An integral of the form ∫ x^(−p) dx used as a benchmark in convergence tests.
If 0 ≤ f ≤ g and ∫ g converges then ∫ f converges; if ∫ f diverges then ∫ g diverges.
Γ(n) = ∫₀^∞ x^(n−1)e^(−x) dx, the continuous extension of the factorial.
B(m,n) = ∫₀¹ x^(m−1)(1−x)^(n−1) dx, expressible through gamma functions.
n! = n(n−1)···1, equal to Γ(n+1) for whole n.
The integral of the vertical distance between an upper and a lower curve over their common interval.
The length of a curve, obtained as the limit of lengths of inscribed chords.
The three-dimensional solid obtained by rotating a plane region about an axis.
A slice of a solid of revolution shaped like a ring, with outer radius R and inner radius r.
The surface traced by rotating a curve about an axis, whose area is an integral of thin bands.
A point where the integrand becomes unbounded, forcing a limit definition of the integral.
